task:
Design a harness for a **turn-based** game (tier 1: the world waits for the agent).

Game: `MiniGrid / BabyAI` — MiniGrid/BabyAI is a synchronous, turn-based gridworld. The mission is the natural-language objective. Each action consumes one step; the episode ends on task success, a hazard/failure, or the step limit. The observation gives the mission, facing direction, carried object, and the currently visible egocentric symbolic grid; unknown cells are occluded. Grid coordinates in the observation use x increasing right and y increasing forward, with the agent at (0,0) and the cell in front at (0,1). Turn left/right changes facing, forward moves one cell, pickup/drop manipulate the facing cell, toggle opens or interacts with it, and done declares completion. Blocked and otherwise invalid in-game actions still consume a step. Success is scored as 0.1 + 0.9 times the fraction of the step budget remaining; failed episodes score zero. The evaluator may provide an environment_id; otherwise a stable SHA-256 mapping selects an audited MiniGrid/BabyAI environment from the declared scenario mix.

Actions:
- left: turn 90 degrees counter-clockwise
- right: turn 90 degrees clockwise
- forward: move one cell forward if it is traversable
- pickup: pick up the object directly in front of you
- drop: drop the carried object in the cell directly in front of you
- toggle: interact with the door or other toggleable object directly in front of you
- done: declare that the mission is complete (the environment may ignore this)
Actions are turn based: one step is consumed per call. Invalid or blocked actions are still environment steps. The view is a 7x7 (or task-configured) egocentric symbolic grid; x increases right and y increases toward the rear of the view.

Model available through `ctx`: `ctx.think(prompt, session_id=...)` — Astra (System-2). Budget: 40 calls
per episode; one call may return a plan of several actions. `ctx.act(action)` applies one action and
returns the next observation. Each episode has a wall-clock deadline of 1800 s, including model
latency (`ctx.budget.remaining()["wall_s"]`); when it passes, or the call budget is used up, the episode
ends with the score reached. Each episode starts cold: fresh `ctx.memory` and fresh module globals.

Evaluation: mean score over the training seeds (the game's own score, see the description), then fewer
System-2 calls, then fewer actions. A candidate can only be selected if none of its training episodes
ends with an error (see the contract: e.g. a TimeoutError from a model call that the harness does not
catch).

What the harness must design: how observations are shown to Astra (full history, a diff, an ASCII map
with a legend, only what changed), what to remember between calls (rules learned, states visited,
plans), how to parse Astra's reply into actions robustly, how many actions to commit per call, when
cheap scripted search or bookkeeping replaces a model call, and how to notice that a plan or belief was
wrong. If the description says that rules or action effects are not given, discovering them by
experiment is part of the task.

A plan must be able to fail and recover. Whatever executes without the model (a compiled build order, a
convention policy, a solver) must check its own effects after each step — `ctx.progress()` counts the
actions since the score and the observation last changed and the actions the game rejected — and, when
the evidence says the plan has stopped working, hand the situation with that evidence to Astra for
re-planning, then verify the new plan the same way. Scenarios the training seeds never show are where a
scripted plan breaks: a candidate with identical scores on every training seed is a scenario-independent
script and will be judged on the unseen validation and held-out seeds.

**Evaluation scope.** The harness is selected on the training seeds of this game and then reported on
unseen seeds of the same game; there is no held-out game. Rules, strategies and search that the game
description or the study establish may be implemented as code once they are verified against
observations — but nothing specific to the training seeds.

## Prior knowledge from the study phase
The study phase researched this game (rules, interface, community strategies). Use it: implement exact
rules, bookkeeping and search as code and put planning and adaptation into Astra prompts — but verify
every claim against observations, because sources can be wrong or outdated for this build of the game.

The full documents are readable in this archive under `prior/` (`prior/strategies.md`, `prior/brief.md`, `prior/interfaces.md`, `prior/study.json`, `prior/ADAPTOR.md`). Below: excerpts within a size budget; every cut is marked `…(truncated; full text in prior/<file>)`.

### study/study.json (summary)
- strategy_summary: Parse the mission into typed predicates and dependencies: then preserves order, after reverses it, and and normally requires both without a fixed order. Maintain a persistent observed map with orientation, inventory, hazards, doors and unknown cells; preserve the initial reference frame for relative descriptions. Use turn-aware search and replan on material new observations, while code enforces interaction preconditions, carrying capacity, hazard rules and step budgets. Astra chooses exploration frontiers, staging cells and plans for ambiguous multi-room tasks. Jev is optional and should answer bounded language-to-object recognition questions, leaving exact decoding, arithmetic, search and bookkeeping to code. Stop on environment termination/truncation and use audited task-specific success extraction, never a model judgment alone.
- scoring: Report success, steps_used, max_steps, remaining_steps, remaining_fraction, raw reward/return, terminated, truncated, environment ID, and seed. For standard sparse tasks use success multiplied by (0.1 + 0.9 * remaining_fraction), equivalent to the usual successful reward 1 - 0.9 * steps/max_steps; keep task-specific raw reward as a diagnostic and never award failed episodes positive credit.
- interface.observation: Default Gymnasium dict: image (uint8 object/color/state codes indexed [x,y,channel] for the visible egocentric grid, commonly 7x7), direction (orientation integer), and mission (text). Decode codes to names and preserve unknown/occluded cells. The base partial view encodes inventory at (V//2,V-1); confirm this for the installed wrapper and do not disclose hidden grid/verifier objects. Add tracked action count, budget, raw reward, terminal flags and a compact history. Full-grid/RGB wrappers are alternatives only if their altered observability is explicitly intended.
- interface.actions: Discrete Actions enum, normally left=0, right=1, forward=2, pickup=3, drop=4, toggle=5, done=6. Actions turn, move one cell, or interact with the adjacent facing object; invalid/blocked actions normally still consume a step. Query the actual action space and task semantics at runtime.

### study/strategies.md
# Strong-play strategies for MiniGrid / BabyAI

Evidence status: written 2026-10-30 from established API/task knowledge and prior research knowledge. Network DNS failed and the evaluator has no MiniGrid installation, so none of the linked web pages or release-specific verifier rules were inspected in this session. Source links are verification targets. Algorithm and model-role recommendations below are proposed engineering choices, not measured winning rates or claims of a community consensus. MiniGrid is a benchmark, not a competitive game: there are no opponents, build orders, or combat counters; the relevant counters address task traps and partial observability.

MiniGrid rewards solving a generated symbolic puzzle under a step budget, while BabyAI adds a natural-language mission and a strict verifier. The primary references are the [MiniGrid documentation](https://minigrid.farama.org/), [environment source](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/tree/master/minigrid/envs), [BabyAI verifier](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/envs/babyai/core/verifier.py), the BabyAI paper ([Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08272)), and the MiniGrid benchmark paper ([Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13831)).

## General execution policy

1. Parse the mission into typed predicates: target object attributes (type, color), required relation (go-to, pick-up, open, put-next), ordering, and any repeated sub-instruction. **Astra prompt:** ask for a short precondition/postcondition plan and a current subgoal. **Code:** keep a mission state machine and action legality checks. **Jev question:** “Which visible object satisfies predicate X?” with a small enum answer.
2. Maintain an egocentric map from observations and turns. Mark walls, doors, hazards, visited cells, object identities, and the agent pose; unknown is distinct from empty. **Code:** coordinate transforms, map bookkeeping, and shortest-path search. **Astra prompt:** choose exploration when the target is not known and revise the map after each observation. **Jev question:** classify each visible cell as wall/open/door/key/target/hazard/unknown.
3. Plan paths with turns included. Before every forward action check the cell ahead; rotate in place to align, then move. Prefer the shortest known safe route and reserve steps for mandatory interactions. **Code:** BFS/A* over known traversable cells with turn cost and carried-object constraints. **Astra prompt:** select which frontier to explore when several routes are possible. **Jev question:** “Is forward safe and legal now?”
4. Interact only when adjacent and facing the object. For pickup, ensure the hand is empty; for drop, ensure the destination is empty and satisfies the verifier; for toggle, distinguish a door from a box. Every failed interaction costs a step. **Code:** precondition checks and action validation. **Astra prompt:** reason about the order of key, door, box, and placement subgoals. **Jev question:** select the legal interaction among `{pickup, drop, toggle, none}`.
5. Stop immediately on success or failure flags. Do not issue `done` as a guess; base MiniGrid usually treats it as an action with no generic success meaning. **Code:** termination handling and score accounting. **Astra prompt:** verify the mission's final condition from the latest observation. **Jev question:** yes/no “Does the latest state satisfy the final predicate?”

## Environment families and useful openings

| Family/task pattern | Strong approach and failure modes | Where to implement |
|---|---|---|
| **Empty / goal navigation / BabyAI GoTo** | A base goal-tile task requires entering the goal cell. BabyAI GoTo normally requires the named object to occupy the cell immediately in front of the agent. MiniGrid GoToObject/GoToDoor are separate tasks whose `done` semantics must be audited. Explore until the target is localized, then route to the correct terminal pose for this ID. | Code for pathfinding and task-specific terminal predicates; Astra for mission interpretation; Jev for ambiguous target recognition. |
| **DoorKey / Unlock** | Find the matching key, pick it up, navigate to the matching locked door, face it, and toggle. Keep the key until the door is opened; do not waste turns trying to walk through a closed door. A key color must match the door color. | Code for inventory and door/key predicates; Astra for route/order under partial visibility; Jev for visible key/door color classification. |
| **MultiRoom / RoomGrid** | Treat doors as graph edges. Explore a room systematically, record doorway orientation and already visited branches, and backtrack rather than repeatedly sweeping the same corridor. Open only the door needed for the current route when step budget is tight. | Code for room/frontier graph and duplicate-visit avoidance; Astra for selecting the next frontier; Jev for “which doorway/room contains the target?” |
| **LavaGap / lava hazards** | Lava is fatal. Infer the safe crossing and do not step onto an unverified lava cell; use walls and the visible gap to align before moving. A one-cell misalignment can end the episode. | Code for hazard mask and forward safety veto; Astra for choosing a crossing route; Jev for fast hazard classification. |
| **DynamicObstacles** | Obstacles update on environment steps, including turns. Audit update/collision order: a currently clear cell is not necessarily safe after the obstacle moves. Re-observe each step, prefer clearance and detours, and respect the restricted action space. There is no wall-clock advantage to thinking faster. | Code for task-specific collision/risk rules and re-planning; Astra for detours; Jev can label current occupancy but cannot certify stochastic future safety. |
| **KeyCorridor / blocked corridors** | Carrying a key or box can be necessary to enter a corridor, and narrow corridors may force a precise order. Avoid dropping an object in a dead-end unless the mission requires it. | Code for capacity and dead-end detection; Astra for ordering; Jev for identifying the only legal next interaction. |
| **Box / UnlockPickup / PutNext** | Boxes may need toggling to reveal contents; “pick up” requires actually carrying the item; “put next” normally requires cardinal adjacency to the referenced object. Check that the destination cell is empty and that the carried object is the required one. | Code for carried-object and placement preconditions; Astra for multi-step dependency planning; Jev for object/relation recognition. |
| **Memory / see-through / hidden-object tasks** | Record a cue (color, object, room, or order) when visible, then use it after moving out of view. Do not treat an occluded cell as empty. | Code for persistent memory keyed by map coordinates/objects; Astra for recalling and applying the cue; Jev for extracting the cue from an observation. |
| **BabyAI instruction levels** | Parse composition explicitly: `A, then B` requires A before B; `A after you B` requires B before A; `A and B` normally requires both without a fixed order. Check strict verifier options before touching later targets. Merely reaching the final object does not establish earlier pickup/open/placement events. | Code for a verifier-aligned subgoal state machine; Astra for parsing and selecting order where allowed; Jev for predicate recognition, never final authoritative success. |

## Search and bookkeeping priorities

Use deterministic BFS/A* over the discovered symbolic map rather than asking a model to count every turn. For navigation include orientation in the search state (`cell, direction`); for manipulation also track inventory, relevant door states, moved objects, and subgoal phase, or decompose into navigation and interaction subproblems. Replan after each material observation, door opening, or dynamic obstacle update. Include every required interaction in the remaining-cost estimate, then add exploration slack; a fixed one-turn reserve is inadequate for a key-door-pickup sequence. A Manhattan distance alone ignores walls, turning, and manipulation and is only a lower bound. These are recommended search methods, grounded in the discrete transition rules, not a requirement to train an RL policy.

When multiple objects match the mission's color/type, first satisfy every location qualifier; only then use reachability/cost as tie-breakers among truly equivalent candidates. Never overwrite an earlier map fact with “empty” from an occluded view. Treat an action that has no visible effect as consumed and investigate the new state rather than repeating it blindly. These are exact rules suitable for code; Astra should handle ambiguity and unexpected layouts; Jev should answer bounded recognition questions, never invent a route or perform arithmetic.

## Verifier-aware tactics and worked plans

The following planning rules reference the [BabyAI verifier](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/envs/babyai/core/verifier.py), [RoomGrid level logic](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/envs/babyai/core/roomgrid_level.py), and [world objects](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/core/world_object.py). Exact strict/done modes and object-description matching require a release audit.

- **Resolve relative language once.** Descriptions such as “on your left” in BabyAI commonly refer to initial agent-relative object sets, not whichever objects happen to be on the agent's left after it turns. Preserve the initial pose frame and mark candidates as they become visible. Astra parses the phrase; code resolves its predicate in that frame. Do not read the verifier's hidden target set into the agent state.
- **Go to the red ball:** enumerate visible/remembered red balls satisfying all qualifiers; choose a reachable cardinal-neighbor pose facing an eligible ball; finish facing it. Do not pick it up merely because pickup is available. Code computes candidate approach poses and routes. Astra chooses a new exploration subgoal if all candidates are unknown. Refer to `GoToInstr` for exact success.
- **Pick up the blue key:** free the hand if needed, navigate to a neighboring pose, face the key, and pickup. Verify inventory changed. In strict task modes picking up a wrong object can fail, so wrong-object pickup is not harmless exploration. Code owns the inventory transition; Astra chooses a safe temporary storage cell when the hand is occupied.
- **Open the red door:** if locked, obtain a red key first; navigate, face, and toggle. Distinguish an opening event from merely standing next to an already open door. An incidental early opening can interfere with later ordered tasks; plan dependencies before toggling mission doors. Standard unlocking retains the key, which matters for the next pickup.

…(truncated; full text in prior/strategies.md)

- **Exploration opening:** parse the mission and inventory first, inspect the initial view, then turn only when a new view is useful. Select a reachable observation frontier rather than blindly spin every four steps. Prefer frontiers/doors that may reveal a target or required key; record checked branches. Code scores travel/turn cost and map coverage; Astra chooses among semantic priorities. Avoid a blanket “never enter unknown” rule that freezes exploration: reveal uncertain cells from safe poses, and audit visibility/hazard rules for the chosen family.
- **Memory opening:** record the cue before leaving it, and associate later branches with the matching object. A branch may terminate the episode upon entry, so obtain enough evidence before committing. Code stores the cue and branch candidates; Astra chooses the matching route. See [Memory](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/envs/memory.py).

For deterministic static tasks, manipulation-free shortest paths on the known map can be exact. An overall optimal plan cannot be guaranteed before exploration exposes the layout. In dynamic tasks observed positions can become stale; label route risk rather than claiming certainty from a one-frame view. If motion cannot be inferred reliably from the observation and action, preserve pose uncertainty rather than adding a fictitious successful forward step.

## Common mistakes and counters

- **Wrong target:** selecting the first red object when the mission says red key, red ball, or a particular room. Counter: typed object predicates and a Jev classification question.
- **Off-by-one interaction:** stopping on the target instead of adjacent and facing it, or toggling while facing the wrong cell. Counter: code-level adjacency/orientation checks and Astra's final-condition review.
- **Door/key deadlock:** trying to pass a locked door, dropping the only key, or carrying the wrong color. Counter: inventory preconditions and a key-door matching table.
- **Hazard death:** treating lava or unseen cells as ordinary floor. Counter: safety veto in code; require explicit observation before forward into a risky cell.
- **Repeated exploration:** turning around in a corridor or reopening already checked rooms. Counter: persistent map/frontier bookkeeping.
- **Ignoring the budget:** finding the goal after spending all steps. Counter: turn-aware shortest paths, reserve steps for interactions, and report remaining steps.
- **Premature completion:** using `done` or stopping after a visually plausible state before the BabyAI verifier event. Counter: explicit subgoal state machine and terminal-success extraction.

## Prompt/Jev interface contract

Astra should receive the mission, decoded visible grid, orientation, carried object, step count/budget, known map summary, and the last action/result. It should return one action from the installed enum plus a brief rationale and updated subgoal; the harness validates the action and ignores prose for control. Prompt priorities: satisfy the exact mission, preserve subgoal ordering and initial-frame qualifiers, minimize actions after ensuring success, and reassess after an unexpected result. A short persistent plan and observed map facts are more useful than re-reading an entire transcript at every step.

Jev is optional for tier 1. Decoding symbolic cell triples, checking a key color, computing adjacency, and counting steps are exact code tasks and should not require a model. Where language-to-object matching is ambiguous, send compact JSON and independent typed questions, for example `candidate_id: {c1,c2,none,unknown}`, `mission_relation: {goto,pickup,open,putnext,unknown}`, or `description_match: {yes,no,unknown}`. Supply code-computed relation facts if asking Jev to choose among them. Jev must not calculate a route, count actions, infer hidden cells, or declare authoritative success; code and environment flags remain decisive. Deterministic legality and hazard checks should be enforced in code even if Jev disagrees. Do not add a continuously running Jev action loop to a game that waits for input.

## Evidence and research context

The BabyAI paper motivates compositional language instructions, procedural tasks, and demonstration/baseline agents; it is useful background, not proof that an LLM will generalize to all held-out layouts. The historical [BabyAI repository](https://github.com/mila-iqia/babyai) and [symbolic bot source](https://github.com/mila-iqia/babyai/blob/master/babyai/bot.py) are verification targets for subgoal-based navigation/manipulation ideas. Do not directly import its planner without checking whether it reads private mission objects or a full map that this benchmark should withhold. The maintained [MiniGrid project](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid) and [task catalog](https://minigrid.farama.org/environments/babyai/) supersede old installation instructions. These research resources were not reachable here, so no source-specific performance numbers or newly researched community claims are asserted.

Validate strategy changes over disjoint seeds with per-family success rate and successful-episode remaining fraction. Compare a minimal deterministic map/path planner plus Astra task parsing against adding optional Jev questions; measure whether added recognition changes actions correctly. Count repeated ineffective interactions, wrong targets, explored cells, and key/door/inventory failures as diagnostics, not bonus rewards. This evaluation proposal belongs in code; Astra interprets systematic failures and proposes changes.

# MiniGrid / BabyAI study

Evidence status (2026-10-30): the evaluator executable was checked directly and is CPython 3.12.3. `pip show minigrid gymnasium numpy pygame` found none installed. Requests to the official documentation, PyPI, and GitHub source failed DNS resolution in this sandbox. Therefore the game details below are a knowledge-based study with explicit source URLs for verification, not a claim that those pages were retrieved or that a particular release was tested. Installation and source-level checks are specified in interfaces.md. No game-playing code was written.

## Game and objective

MiniGrid is a family of small, procedural, grid-world environments maintained by the Farama Foundation. BabyAI is an instruction-following task suite incorporated into modern MiniGrid. These are single-agent benchmark environments, not an online service. A mission can require reaching a goal, approaching an object, picking something up, opening/unlocking doors, placing one object next to another, remembering a cue, or performing several instructions in order. The mission and environment family determine success; there is no universal “walk onto the green square” rule. [B1, B2, B5]

The agent occupies one cell and faces one of four directions. Walls, closed doors, and most objects block forward movement. The agent can carry only one object at a time. A matching-color key unlocks a locked door; ordinary unlocking does not consume the key. Doors, balls, keys, and boxes have colors, and some tasks distinguish otherwise identical objects by location. Toggling a box can reveal its contents. Lava can be entered but is fatal. Not all apparently traversable cells are safe. [B3, B4]

Most environments give a small, egocentric, partially observable symbolic view, normally 7×7 cells, a direction, and a textual mission. The “image” in the default observation is an array of object/color/state codes, not RGB pixels. Occlusion and unseen cells must be preserved in text; unseen is not empty. Some tasks deliberately change visibility, size, action semantics, or reward. [B1, B3, B6]

## Actions and their costs

The standard action enum is below. Read the installed enum rather than hard-coding assumptions for every subclass. Each submitted action normally increments the environment step counter, including a blocked move, unsuccessful interaction, or otherwise ineffective action. [B3, B4]

| ID | Name | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | left | Turn 90° counterclockwise in place. |
| 1 | right | Turn 90° clockwise in place. |
| 2 | forward | Move one cell in the facing direction if allowed. |
| 3 | pickup | Pick up the immediately front object if pickupable and the hand is empty. |
| 4 | drop | Drop the carried object into an empty front cell. |
| 5 | toggle | Interact with the front object: open/close a door, unlock with a matching key, open a box. |
| 6 | done | Base MiniGrid usually does nothing beyond spending a step; some task/verifier modes use an explicit completion action. Never assume this means success. |

There is no standard backward, strafe, diagonal, click-object, or teleport action. Interactions require facing the adjacent cell. Some environment families expose fewer actions or override them; DynamicObstacles and specialized tasks need explicit audits. See interfaces.md for family restrictions. [B3, B5]

BabyAI distinctions matter: “go to” generally means becoming adjacent to and facing a qualifying object, “pick up” means actually carrying it, “open” means the required door opening event, and “put next” means a qualifying placement beside the destination, usually cardinal adjacency rather than diagonals. Exact event checks, strict ordering, and explicit-done behavior belong to the installed instruction verifier. Arbitrarily dropping beside an object or standing nearby is not a substitute for checking that verifier. [B7]

## Score, progress, and termination

For many standard sparse-reward tasks, success reward is

`1 - 0.9 * (step_count / max_steps)`.

Failure and unsuccessful timeout normally yield zero. Thus successful shorter episodes score better, and successful episodes near the limit still yield about 0.1. This is not a safe assumption for every registered environment: distance shaping, intermediate rewards, special failure rewards, and task-specific termination exist. Restrict the benchmark to audited sparse-success families or define a separate per-family success extractor. [B3, B5]

Report `success`, `steps_used`, `max_steps`, `remaining_steps = max(0, max_steps - steps_used)`, `remaining_fraction`, raw reward/return, `terminated`, and `truncated`. For a mixed-size benchmark use the standard success reward as the primary scalar for the chosen sparse families: `score = success * (0.1 + 0.9 * remaining_fraction)`. Also publish success rate and mean remaining fraction among successes; do not give a failed episode positive credit merely because it ended early. Compare raw remaining steps only within the same task/budget. Mission subgoals and explored cells are diagnostic progress, not score. [B3; benchmark design recommendation]

The Gymnasium API separates terminal events (`terminated`, such as success or lava death) from time limits (`truncated`). Neither flag alone means success. Both may be true on a successful last allowed step, so retain terminal success in that case. Stop stepping once either is true and reset for the next episode. Maximum budgets depend on environment and dimensions; read the actual instance and account for an outer TimeLimit wrapper. [B3, B8]

## Pace and model roles

**Tier 1 is correct.** The environment advances through synchronous `step(action)` calls. It does not move while the model is thinking. Even moving-obstacle tasks update in steps, not according to elapsed wall time. Astra can deliberate for seconds or a minute without spending in-game time. A surrounding evaluator can impose an independent wall-clock timeout; none was supplied. Render FPS is not a decision deadline. [B3, B5, B8]

There is no finite intrinsic decision latency limit. In study.json, `decision_latency_s: -1.0` is an explicitly documented sentinel for “unbounded by game mechanics”; it is not a literal negative timeout. Do not implement it as an immediate timeout. Jev is optional for this tier and should not control an asynchronous action loop.

### adaptor/ADAPTOR.md
# MiniGrid / BabyAI adaptor

This is a Tier 1 adaptor for the official `minigrid==3.0.0` Gymnasium package. Importing
`minigrid` registers the local MiniGrid and BabyAI environments; no server, account, GUI,
network connection, or credentials are needed. The adaptor constructs a fresh environment on
each `reset(seed)` and closes it at episode end.

When the evaluator passes `env_id`, `environment_id`, or `id`, that ID is used directly. If it
does not, the external seed is mapped with SHA-256 domains `minigrid-adaptor-v1:scenario:<seed>`
and `minigrid-adaptor-v1:reset:<seed>`. The first digest selects uniformly from this ordered,
audited allowlist: `MiniGrid-Empty-Random-6x6-v0`, `MiniGrid-DoorKey-6x6-v0`,
`MiniGrid-MultiRoom-N2-S4-v0`, `BabyAI-GoToRedBallGrey-v0`, `BabyAI-GoToObj-v0`, and
`BabyAI-PickupLoc-v0`. The second digest is the Gymnasium reset seed. This avoids Python's
process-randomized `hash()` and registry order. Reset and finish records are appended under
`runtime/episodes.jsonl` with the external seed, actual reset seed, ID, kwargs, and package
versions.

The model receives the mission, facing direction, carried object when visible, and a decoded
egocentric symbolic grid from the public Gymnasium observation. `unknown` cells remain unknown;
the hidden world and verifier state are never exposed. Grid cells are reported in the image's
`[x,y,channel]` convention, with relative x increasing right and y increasing toward the rear.
The action vocabulary is `left`, `right`, `forward`, `pickup`, `drop`, `toggle`, and `done`.
Malformed adaptor actions are ignored and reported in the next observation; valid but blocked
actions are passed through and consume a normal environment step.

For audited sparse tasks, success is a positive terminal reward or explicit `info["success"]`.
The primary score is zero on failure and `0.1 + 0.9 * remaining_steps / max_steps` on success.
`info()` and `score_breakdown()` retain success, steps, budget, remaining fraction, raw reward and
return, terminal flags, ID, and both seeds. This preserves headroom for faster successful play.

Admission checks covered each selected family: Empty-Random (goal reach), DoorKey (key, door,
goal), MultiRoom (room traversal), BabyAI GoToRedBallGrey, BabyAI GoToObj, and BabyAI PickupLoc.
All six use the installed sparse verifier/reward convention: failure and timeout return zero,
while the successful verifier transition returns a positive reward; no shaping or custom wrapper
is applied. The train, held-out, and validation seed groups use the same family mix (two Empty,
two DoorKey, and one of each other family).

The adaptor has no intrinsic wall-clock deadline: Gymnasium changes state only when `step()` is
called. Rendering is deliberately disabled. Package versions are pinned in `requirements.txt`;
install it in the evaluator interpreter before validation.

The recommended adaptor is the official Python environment API. MiniGrid is a local, deterministic benchmark suite, so it has no server, account, matchmaking service, or game credentials. The authoritative project is the Farama Foundation repository and its documentation ([project](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid), [basic usage](https://minigrid.farama.org/content/basic_usage/), [environment catalog](https://minigrid.farama.org/environments/minigrid/)). ## Interface comparison

| Interface | What it exposes and latency | Maturity/cost | Legal/operational risk | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gymnasium API (`gym.make("MiniGrid-...-v0")`)** | Synchronous `reset(seed)` and `step(action)`; structured dict observation (`image`, `direction`, `mission`) and scalar reward/termination. A call advances exactly one game step; model thinking does not advance the world. | Official, maintained, free; CPU-only for normal use. | No online service or anti-cheat issue. Must follow package license and pin versions. | **Choose this.** It is the benchmark interface and gives exact actions and state without vision or input injection. |
| Direct MiniGrid internals (`env.unwrapped`, grid/world objects) | Adds exact grid cells, agent position/direction, carried object, mission and step counter; useful for debugging and a text-state serializer. | Official source but semi-private, version-sensitive; free and negligible latency. | No external risk; coupling to internals can break after upgrades. | Use only inside an optional debug/diagnostic path; the playing adaptor should rely on the public observation. |
| Official wrappers | `FullyObsWrapper` gives a full symbolic grid; `ViewSizeWrapper` changes egocentric window; `RGBImgPartialObsWrapper`/`RGBImgObsWrapper` produce pixels; `ImgObsWrapper`, `FlatObsWrapper`, and `OneHotPartialObsWrapper` alter representation. See [wrapper API](https://minigrid.farama.org/api/wrappers/) and [source](https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid/blob/master/minigrid/wrappers.py). | Maintained with MiniGrid; free; wrapper overhead is tiny. | Wrapper changes task observability and can invalidate a benchmark's intended partial-observation setting. | Use only when the evaluator explicitly permits it. A textual serializer around the default dict is the safest standard. |
| RL/bot libraries (Stable-Baselines3, CleanRL, RLlib) | These consume a Gymnasium env and issue the same discrete actions; vectorized environments can batch episodes but add no new state access. | Mature general RL tooling, free/open source, but extra dependencies and policy inference latency. | A pretrained policy may be trained on a different ID/version and silently exploit full observations. | Optional offline baseline only; not needed for the Astra harness. |
